extracted.intended_audience: researchers, data producers, repository managers, publishers, funders, and tool/software builders involved in scholarly data management and stewardship
extracted.subtask_description: High-level guiding principles for making scholarly data and related research objects Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR). Intended to guide data producers, repositories, and tool-builders in evaluating and improving data stewardship and machine-actionability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findable (F)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be Findable: F1. (meta)data are assigned a globally unique and persistent identifier; F2. data are described with rich metadata (defined by R1 below); F3. metadata clearly and explicitly include the identifier of the data it describes; F4. (meta)data are registered or indexed in a searchable resource.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findability requires persistent identifiers (DOIs, Handles, stable URLs) that resolve to landing pages with metadata and access information. Metadata should be sufficiently rich (see Reusability/R1) and include the data's identifier. Data and metadata should be indexed/registered in searchable resources (repositories, discovery indices). Examples: Dataverse issues DOIs/Handles and landing pages; wwPDB and UniProt provide stable identifiers and searchable indexes. Rich landing-page metadata supports both human and machine discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible (A)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be Accessible: A1. (meta)data are retrievable by their identifier using a standardized communications protocol; A1.1 the protocol is open, free, and universally implementable; A1.2 the protocol allows for an authentication and authorization procedure, where necessary; A2. metadata are accessible, even when the data are no longer available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility requires use of standardized, preferably open and universally implementable protocols (e.g., HTTP, web APIs) to retrieve (meta)data by identifier. Protocols must support authentication/authorization when needed (for sensitive data). Even if the underlying data are restricted or removed, metadata should remain accessible to enable discovery and understanding of the resource. Examples: Dataverse and Open PHACTS provide machine-accessible interfaces and tokens for restricted data; wwPDB hosts stable FTP/HTTP access to entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interoperable (I)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be Interoperable: I1. (meta)data use a formal, accessible, shared, and broadly applicable language for knowledge representation; I2. (meta)data use vocabularies that follow FAIR principles; I3. (meta)data include qualified references to other (meta)data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interoperability emphasizes formal, shared representation languages (RDF, XML, JSON-LD, ontologies) and community vocabularies/ontologies to enable integration and automated processing. Vocabularies used should themselves follow FAIR principles (publishable, versioned, resolvable). Metadata should include clear, qualified links/references to related (meta)data (cross-references). Examples: UniProt RDF using shared vocabularies, ISA RDF/JSON for structured metadata, Open PHACTS using VoID and ontologies; where no community vocabulary exists, publish an extension or a new vocabulary following FAIR (I2 guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reusable (R)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be Reusable: R1. meta(data) are richly described with a plurality of accurate and relevant attributes; R1.1. (meta)data are released with a clear and accessible data usage license; R1.2. (meta)data are associated with detailed provenance; R1.3. (meta)data meet domain-relevant community standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusability requires rich, accurate metadata describing content, context, and methods (provenance) to enable correct interpretation and reuse. Clear, accessible licensing must be provided so users (and machines) can determine permitted uses. Metadata should record detailed provenance (who generated what, when, how) and conform to community-accepted standards/ schemas where available. Examples: Dataverse provides citation metadata and license info; wwPDB and UniProt include provenance and domain standards; ISA framework supports domain-relevant structured metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-actionability (continuum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital objects and their (meta)data should be 'machine-actionable' to varying degrees—i.e., provide information enabling an autonomously-acting computational agent to (a) identify the type of object, (b) determine if it is useful for the agent's task via metadata/data interrogation, (c) determine if it is usable (license/consent/access constraints), and (d) take appropriate action—analogous to what a human would do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine-actionability is a continuum: partial machine-readability (e.g., type identification) up to full autonomous use. Achieving machine-actionability favors general-purpose, open technologies and shared semantics over bespoke parsers. Design metadata and data representations so agents can parse type, semantics, license, provenance, and access mechanisms programmatically. Examples and tools: RDF, JSON-LD, standardized APIs, and community vocabularies; the FAIR principles are intended as steps along this continuum rather than a binary state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply FAIR to all scholarly digital research objects
rubrics_metrics.description: FAIR principles apply not only to 'data' sensu stricto but also to algorithms, tools, workflows, and other scholarly digital research objects; all components of the research process should be identifiable, describable, discoverable, and reusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing workflows, code, or tools, treat them as research objects: assign identifiers, provide rich metadata (including inputs/outputs and provenance), use interoperable representation formats, and include clear licensing. This supports transparency, reproducibility and reuse. Examples: ISA and workflow publication practices; FAIRDOM integrates models and data with persistent URLs and RDF metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles precede implementation (non-prescriptiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAIR Guiding Principles are high-level guidance that precede implementation choices and are not themselves a standard or specification; they do not mandate specific technologies or formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementers should use the FAIR principles to evaluate whether implementation choices support Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability, but are free to adopt technologies and standards appropriate for their domain and context. FAIRness can be attained incrementally and modularly; where domain vocabularies are lacking, publish extensions or new vocabularies following FAIR. Avoid judging FAIRness by adherence to a single technology; focus on the principles' intent (e.g., persistent IDs, rich metadata, open protocols).
